title: What Loads Into the Window, and What Doesn't

questions.prompt: You paste a long log, ask about its start, and later ask about it again — Claude Code can no longer see that part. What happened?
options: A bug — the log should stay readable once pasted
The block filled up: later content pushed the earlier part out, so the tool is reading from what is left
The log was deleted from disk
questions.explanation: The fixed-size block holds everything the tool sees, so new content evicts old content — it is a budget running out, not a capability failing. Option A is tempting because the words are still on your screen, but the transcript on disk is not the same as the block the tool reads. Option C assigns intent where there is only a limit. Option D mistakes the window for storage.

questions.prompt: Which input costs the most room per turn once it is sitting in the block?
options: A word in the system prompt
A long file the tool just read
questions.explanation: Cost rises from a line of chat to a short result to a long file read, so a file the tool read is the most expensive per turn. Option D is tempting because a tool result feels like a small detail, but a short result is medium and a long read is the heavy one. Options A and B are the cheap end of the ordering.

questions.prompt: You ask for a small edit. You never see an explicit "reading" message — only the edit result. What is true?
options: It did not read the file; it edited blind
It read the file during the act step; that read lives in the block for the rest of the session and costs every turn
It read the file but discarded the read immediately
File reads never enter the block
questions.explanation: A hidden read is still a read: it happens during the act step and then sits in the block, costing room on every later turn. Option A is tempting when no reading message appears, but the edit could not have been made without the read. Option C assumes the read is transient when it is retained. Option D contradicts the whole model.

questions.prompt: Your test command prints megabytes of output, and you run it every few turns. What is the effect on the block?
options: Only the first run costs; later runs are free
Each run's output stays in the block and is re-paid every following turn, crowding out earlier content
The tool compacts just that output automatically, so it is free
The tool refuses to run it
questions.explanation: A giant output dump is the most expensive kind of content, and it is re-paid on every turn it remains. Option A is tempting because the command itself ran once, but its output persists. Option C invents targeted compaction that the lesson does not describe. Option D is not the failure mode — the block fills, the tool does not decline.
